labs.title: Vulnversity
labs.summary: Bypassed a web upload extension filter, obtained a www-data reverse shell, and used SUID-enabled systemctl to demonstrate root command execution.

attackPath.title: Discover exposed web application
attackPath.detail: Enumerated services and found an upload form under /internal/ on the lab web server.

attackPath.title: Investigate upload validation
attackPath.detail: Used Burp Intruder to probe filename extensions; spotted URL encoding of the dot (%2e) in an unsuccessful request and adjusted the payload format. The .phtml upload was then accepted.

attackPath.title: Gain initial shell
attackPath.detail: Configured a PHP reverse-shell callback to the Kali VPN tun0 address and listened with netcat; trigger produced uid=33(www-data).

attackPath.title: Find privileged executable
attackPath.detail: Enumerated Linux permissions and confirmed /bin/systemctl was owned by root with SUID set.

attackPath.title: Prove root command execution
attackPath.detail: Created a temporary oneshot systemd unit whose ExecStart ran id; output file contained uid=0(root).

attackPath.title: Inspect protected data
attackPath.detail: Used the root-executed service to list /root, confirming root.txt existed; practiced the SUID Bash approach. User later marked the room complete.

labs.methodology:
## Approach
- Locate the exposed web functionality and validate whether the server allows executable file types.
- Inspect the actual multipart filename Burp sends; do not use the HTTP 200 code alone as proof of a successful upload.
- Configure the callback to the attacker VPN interface (`tun0`), not to the target or the public IP.
- Once in the `www-data` context, enumerate local privilege boundaries and verify a suspected misconfiguration through a minimal proof of execution.

recon.title: HTTP upload filter
recon.detail: The application reported `Extension not allowed` even though Intruder requests returned HTTP 200. Burp sent `filename="shell%2ephtml"` during an unsuccessful extension test.

recon.title: Kali VPN and reverse connection
recon.detail: The active Kali VPN interface was `tun0`. The PHP script called back to a listener on port 1234, and its shell identified as `www-data`.

recon.title: Root-owned SUID systemctl
recon.detail: The permission string was confirmed as `-rwsr-xr-x`, with root as owner.

recon.title: Root execution confirmation
recon.detail: A temporary systemd service ran `id` as root. This proved root command execution, not that the original reverse shell changed identity.

recon.title: Protected directory
recon.detail: The root-executed service listed `/root`; the listing included `root.txt` (33 bytes). The flag value is deliberately not stored.

findings.title: Executable upload accepted by web application
findings.evidence: A `.phtml` upload succeeded after correcting the transmitted multipart filename, and executing the uploaded PHP produced a `www-data` shell.
findings.rootCause: Executable file upload was permitted in a web-accessible location and processed as server-side PHP.
findings.impact: Remote code execution with web-service privileges.
findings.remediation: Use strict allowlists and verify file content server-side; store uploads outside executable directories; disable script execution for upload paths.
findings.validation: Confirm disallowed scripts cannot be uploaded or executed.

findings.title: Root-owned systemctl with SUID bit
findings.evidence: `ls -l /bin/systemctl` showed `-rwsr-xr-x ... root root`. A temporary service executed `id` and wrote `uid=0(root)` to a file.
findings.rootCause: SUID on a service-management utility allowed privileged service operations to be requested by a lower-privileged user in this lab.
findings.impact: Privilege escalation from web-service access to root-level command execution.
findings.remediation: Remove the SUID bit from systemctl and audit authorization policy and privileged services.
findings.validation: With an unprivileged account, verify custom root service creation and execution are denied.

learnings: TCP SYN scan (`-sS`) learns port state from TCP responses without a completed handshake; open does not mean vulnerable.
Burp Intruder can vary a multipart filename; inspect the raw request because encoded `%2e` may not be treated as a literal extension dot.
HTTP 200 means the request was handled; the response body determines whether the upload succeeded.
For a reverse shell, the callback is the reachable Kali VPN address on `tun0`, and the listener port must match.
SUID on a root-owned executable can confer an effective root identity; privileged operations still depend on the program and authorization.
systemctl requests service actions; a `.service` unit defines what systemd executes. The proof used output redirected to `/tmp`.
Root command execution in a separate service is not the same as converting an existing `www-data` shell to root.
A file readable by mode bits may still be inaccessible when a parent directory lacks traversal permission.
difficulties: Needed help interpreting the SYN/RST handshake and what closed versus filtered implies.
Initially the multipart filename used `%2e` instead of a literal dot; identified by inspecting Burp Raw Request.
Needed guided explanation and command construction for a systemd oneshot service and a privileged shell.
Actual root flag bytes were not supplied; the user reported finishing the lab.
labs.report:
## Outcome
Guided exploitation chain completed. An executable upload produced a `www-data` reverse shell. A SUID-root `systemctl` executed a temporary service with `uid=0(root)`.

## Confidence / boundaries
Root-level command execution was directly verified. The transcript does not contain the final interactive root-shell identity or flag contents, so neither is asserted as independently evidenced. The room was subsequently marked complete by the learner.

## Defensive interpretation
Two unrelated controls failed: an upload directory executed attacker-supplied PHP, and a service manager control executable was SUID root. Restricting either step disrupts the demonstrated chain.

labs.title: Kenobi
labs.summary: Combined anonymous SMB disclosure, ProFTPD mod_copy, an NFS export, and SSH key authentication; investigated a custom SUID menu executable and PATH hijacking.

attackPath.title: Enumerate the network
attackPath.detail: A full TCP scan found 11 open ports, including FTP (21), SSH (22), SMB (139/445), RPC/NFS (111/2049) and HTTP (80).

attackPath.title: Read anonymous SMB share
attackPath.detail: Nmap SMB scripts returned no share list, but an anonymous SMB connection exposed log.txt with Kenobi SSH-key paths and configuration clues.

attackPath.title: Research FTP version
attackPath.detail: Nmap identified ProFTPD 1.3.5. SearchSploit listed mod_copy exploit material; examined the file-copy technique instead of assuming version alone proves vulnerability.

attackPath.title: Verify FTP copy operations
attackPath.detail: The FTP service exposed SITE CPFR/CPTO. A source-file probe was accepted; the learner later reported the SSH key copy succeeded.

attackPath.title: Retrieve file through NFS
attackPath.detail: NFS exported /var. Mounted it, and used the FTP service to copy the key into /var/tmp; accessed the file through the mount.

attackPath.title: Authenticate as kenobi
attackPath.detail: Copied the key to Kali with restrictive permissions and successfully logged into SSH as kenobi.

attackPath.title: Investigate local escalation
attackPath.detail: SUID enumeration uncovered /usr/bin/menu. `strings` revealed `setuid`, `system` and commands resolved through PATH; a PATH-hijack workflow was practiced with guidance, but final root-shell output was not supplied.

labs.methodology:
## Approach
- Enumerate all TCP ports and service versions first, rather than guessing the correct exploit.
- Treat anonymous access, file paths and service configuration as clues that may connect services.
- Research version-specific public vulnerability material; validate the required server behavior before relying on an exploit.
- Use evidence from SMB, FTP and NFS to construct a multi-service path to SSH authentication.
- After a user shell, look for unusual SUID executables and understand program behavior before attempting escalation.

recon.title: SMB shares and log.txt
recon.detail: The SMB NSE scripts produced no share enumeration output. An anonymous SMB session worked, and `log.txt` included `/home/kenobi/.ssh/id_rsa` and an anonymous share definition. The ProFTPD sample configuration is a clue, not proof of the active configuration.

commands.label: Retrieve share file from SMB prompt

recon.title: FTP service version and research
recon.detail: Nmap identified ProFTPD 1.3.5. The local SearchSploit listing included files 37262.rb, 36803.py, 49908.py and 36742.txt.

recon.title: FTP SITE functionality
recon.detail: The student reported that `SITE HELP` included CPFR and CPTO and `SITE CPFR /etc/passwd` returned the anticipated positive source response. The separate SSH-key copy was reported successful.

recon.title: NFS export and key retrieval
recon.detail: The NFS export list included `/var`; the `/var` mount exposed `/var/tmp`. SSH authentication with the copied key succeeded.

recon.title: SUID menu and PATH
recon.detail: `strings` displayed `setuid`, `system`, `curl -I localhost`, `uname -r`, and `ifconfig`. The real `curl` resolved to `/usr/bin/curl`. A PATH replacement technique was taught; final root identity output was not shared.

findings.title: Anonymous SMB disclosure
findings.evidence: Anonymous SMB access revealed `log.txt` containing SSH key locations and service configurations.
findings.rootCause: The `[anonymous]` Samba share allowed guest access to operational information.
findings.impact: Information disclosure helped construct an attack path into the machine.
findings.remediation: Restrict guest shares and remove sensitive administrative files from anonymously accessible locations.
findings.validation: Verify anonymous users cannot read internal configuration or credential-location information.

findings.title: Unauthenticated ProFTPD mod_copy file copying
findings.evidence: ProFTPD 1.3.5 exposed `SITE CPFR` and `SITE CPTO`; a server-side copy of an SSH private key into `/var/tmp` was reported successful.
findings.rootCause: Affected `mod_copy` behavior permitted file copying on the server without FTP authentication in the lab.
findings.impact: Sensitive private-key material became available through another exported path.
findings.remediation: Update or patch ProFTPD, disable unneeded mod_copy, and restrict filesystem privileges.
findings.validation: Verify unauthenticated SITE copy operations no longer succeed.

findings.title: NFS export enabled retrieval of copied key
findings.evidence: `showmount -e` returned `/var`; mounting it enabled access to the copied file in `/var/tmp`. SSH access as kenobi was then confirmed.
findings.rootCause: Network-accessible export combined with an unsafe server-side file-copy operation.
findings.impact: Compromise of an interactive Linux user account via SSH key.
findings.remediation: Limit NFS exports to necessary directories and authorized clients; protect sensitive copied material and key files.
findings.validation: Verify the export is restricted and sensitive files are not retrievable.

learnings: An Nmap port scan identifies possible attack surface; NSE scripts can yield no results despite a reachable SMB service.
SMB guest access can leak file paths and configuration details; those details are clues, not automatic exploits.
Identify an exact service version, research applicable vulnerabilities, and validate actual behavior before exploitation.
ProFTPD SITE CPFR and CPTO perform server-side file copies; their unauthenticated use was tested in this lab.
NFS exports can be enumerated with showmount and mounted to a local path; network filesystem access follows separate permission rules.
SSH private-key authentication uses `ssh -i`; copying a key locally requires restrictive file permissions such as chmod 600.
A nonstandard SUID binary is worth examining; strings reveals clues about referenced functions and invoked commands, but does not prove exploitability.
`PATH` is searched left to right. `export PATH=/home/kenobi/tools/:$PATH` adds a preferred directory while retaining previous entries.
Privilege-escalation discovery and independent shell-script construction still need deliberate practice.
difficulties: Initial smb-enum-shares and smb-enum-users scripts returned no shares; an smbclient fallback resolved it.
Needed guided prompting to choose ProFTPD, connect information from SMB and NFS, and recognize an attack point.
Needed explanation of exploit database entries, FTP SITE commands, NFS mounting and SUID PATH hijacking.
User can explain high-level attack chains but said they are not yet confident constructing shell scripts/commands independently.
A post-hijack `id` output confirming an effective-root interactive shell was not provided.
labs.report:
## Outcome
Anonymous SMB gave access to `log.txt`, which disclosed a private-key path. Nmap identified ProFTPD 1.3.5; the lab's FTP server accepted mod_copy commands. A key copy into an NFS-exported path was reported successful, and SSH login as `kenobi` was confirmed.

## Local escalation investigation
A nonstandard root SUID binary, `/usr/bin/menu`, appeared in the enumeration. `strings` exposed `setuid`, `system`, and relative command names. A PATH hijack was taught and its mechanism discussed, but the final execution identity was not recorded in the supplied transcript. Therefore the site does not claim independently verified root access from that step.

## Learning gap
The user explicitly requested more practice independently identifying attack points and constructing Bash commands rather than being given the next exploit.

guides.title: Attack-point discovery workflow
guides.summary: Enumerate broadly, connect findings, investigate promising services, and validate instead of guessing.
takeaways: An open port is a lead, not proof of a vulnerability.
Do not treat a matching CVE as confirmed exploitation.
Ask: what do I control, what can I read/write, and what new boundary could this cross?
guides.content:
## Practical decision loop
1. **Discover**: list ports, services, web routes and shares.
2. **Identify**: probe versions, permissions, authentication and exposed files.
3. **Research**: use local exploit references and vendor information for the actual version/configuration.
4. **Hypothesize**: explain which condition could be exploited and what additional access it would provide.
5. **Validate**: test the suspected weakness inside the lab and record actual responses.
6. **Chain**: ask whether one service's access or output helps reach another service.

At each step, separate observed facts from guesses. The Kenobi chain combined an SMB path disclosure, ProFTPD copying, an NFS export and SSH authentication. The learner said independently selecting the next attack point is still a priority for practice.

examples.title: Identify software on discovered ports
examples.explanation: Map service identity and default script output before choosing a hypothesis.

pitfalls: A walkthrough can hide the discovery work.
A sample config file does not guarantee the live service uses the same configuration.

guides.title: Nmap TCP scan basics
guides.summary: Interpret TCP open, closed and filtered states and use service detection after port discovery.
takeaways: An RST normally suggests a closed TCP port but some firewalls send resets.
Open only means a service is accepting connection attempts.
guides.content:
## Response logic
- **Open**: SYN generally receives SYN/ACK.
- **Closed**: SYN generally receives RST.
- **Filtered**: probes may get no response or certain ICMP errors; a firewall may also actively reject.

`-sS` performs a TCP SYN scan without a normal completed connection; `-sT` uses the OS connect API. Both are detectable. `-p-` scans the full TCP port range, while `-sV` identifies the software behind an open port.

examples.explanation: Enumerate all TCP ports in an authorized lab.

pitfalls: A banner may be misleading or reflect backported patches.

guides.title: Burp Intruder: upload extension checks
guides.summary: Inspect the actual multipart filename and application response when testing upload restrictions.
takeaways: The actual outgoing HTTP request matters more than the payload list you intended.
guides.content:
## The Vulnversity pitfall
A request contained `filename="shell%2ephtml"`. `%2e` is the encoded dot; the multipart upload handler did not accept it as the intended `.phtml` extension. A literal `filename="shell.phtml"` was needed.

HTTP **200** alone was not proof of acceptance; the body said `Extension not allowed`. Place the payload marker around the extension text or disable dot encoding, then inspect the **Raw Request** and **Response**.

examples.title: Correct multipart filename
examples.explanation: A literal extension in the filename parameter.

pitfalls: The endpoint may return HTTP 200 for both success and failure.

guides.title: PHP reverse shell and VPN callback
guides.summary: The server calls back to a listener on the reachable Kali VPN address.
takeaways: Uploading a PHP file and executing it are separate steps.
A reverse shell inherits the web service process permissions.
guides.content:
## Connection direction
A reverse shell makes a connection **from the target to Kali**. In the Vulnversity lab, the PHP script called `fsockopen($ip, $port, ...)` and then launched a shell through `proc_open()`.

The callback address was the Kali `tun0` VPN address, not the target address or a public IP. Matching the listener port was necessary. The shell ran as `www-data`, not root.

examples.explanation: Find the IP reachable from the TryHackMe lab.

examples.title: Listen for a connection
examples.explanation: Start a TCP listener matching the PHP callback port.

pitfalls: Verify that the VPN tunnel is active.
A non-interactive /bin/sh may lack job control and a TTY.

guides.title: SUID and Linux privilege boundaries
guides.summary: A root-owned SUID executable can run with effective root privileges; the program still needs unsafe behavior.
takeaways: Real UID and effective UID can differ.
Ownership plus execute permission is not the same as SUID.
guides.content:
## Permissions
`-rwsr-xr-x root root /path/program` shows an `s` in the owner's execute position. SUID typically makes the executable process run with its owner's effective UID, while the invoking user's real UID remains unchanged.

This does **not** automatically make every SUID program exploitable. Normal programs like `passwd` legitimately require elevated operations. Nonstandard binaries such as Kenobi's `/usr/bin/menu` deserve closer investigation.

examples.explanation: Find regular files with user SUID set while suppressing error messages.

examples.title: Check owner and mode
examples.explanation: Read the s position and root owner.

guides.title: systemctl, oneshot services and root proofs
guides.summary: A unit file defines a command; systemctl asks systemd to start it.
takeaways: Privileged command execution and an interactive root shell are distinct.
Use the minimum necessary proof and remove test artifacts after a lab.
guides.content:
## Mechanism learned in Vulnversity
A `.service` file has an `ExecStart` instruction describing what systemd should run. In the lab, root-owned SUID `systemctl` enabled privileged service actions. A temporary oneshot service wrote the output of `id` to a file in `/tmp`.

The output contained `uid=0(root)`: proof the service command ran as root. The original `www-data` shell did not automatically become root. `daemon-reload` is used when changing unit definitions, and `start`/`restart` runs a service.

examples.title: Check proof output
examples.explanation: Look for the effective execution identity.

pitfalls: Do not leave SUID Bash copies or temporary privileged services behind.

guides.title: SMB guest enumeration
guides.summary: List SMB shares and inspect anonymous content; use a fallback if NSE scripts show nothing.
takeaways: No script output is not proof there are no shares.
Read retrieved files for usernames, paths and references to other services.
guides.content:
## Practical approach
SMB commonly uses TCP 445 or 139. Kenobi's `smb-enum-shares.nse` and `smb-enum-users.nse` produced no share output, even though the ports were open. A separate `smbclient` attempt without a password worked.

An anonymous share contained `log.txt`, which exposed internal configuration clues and an SSH key path. Guest access is therefore a potential information-disclosure issue.

guides.title: SearchSploit and exploit validation
guides.summary: Search by product/version, inspect references, then test requirements rather than blindly running an exploit.
takeaways: A matching result is not a confirmed vulnerability.
Understand what access or file operation the candidate exploit provides.
guides.content:
## Kenobi example
Nmap identified `ProFTPD 1.3.5`. SearchSploit listed four relevant records: command-execution variants and a file-copy reference. The file-copy reference was relevant because the SMB log had disclosed a private-key path.

Research supplied a hypothesis. The server's actual `SITE` response and subsequent reported copy established whether the behavior existed in the lab.

examples.title: Search local exploit references
examples.explanation: Look up version-specific exploit material.

examples.title: Read a reference
examples.explanation: Examine details without blindly executing a script.

pitfalls: Check enabled modules, filesystem permissions and potential patches.

guides.title: ProFTPD SITE CPFR / CPTO
guides.summary: FTP SITE carries server-specific commands; mod_copy can copy files entirely on the server.
takeaways: Server-side copying does not transfer the file to Kali.
The FTP daemon must have permission to read the source and write the destination.
guides.content:
## Protocol behavior
`SITE` introduces a site-specific FTP command. ProFTPD's `mod_copy` provides `CPFR` (**copy from**) and `CPTO` (**copy to**). In affected configurations, FTP clients may invoke these without authenticating.

A `350` response indicates a source accepted and a destination is expected; `250` means the operation was successful. Kenobi's vulnerable service exposed the commands, enabling an SSH key to be copied to a path that another service exposed.

examples.explanation: FTP control commands are plain text over a TCP connection.

examples.title: Inspect SITE functionality
examples.explanation: Identify supported site-specific commands and test source acceptance.

pitfalls: A recognized SITE command alone does not prove exploitable copying.

guides.title: NFS export discovery and mounting
guides.summary: NFS exposes server directories as mountable filesystems with their own access controls.
takeaways: The local mount point corresponds to the remote export path.
Files still have ownership and permission controls.
guides.content:
## Kenobi connection
`showmount -e` listed `/var` as an exported path. Kali mounted this path under `/mnt/kenobi`. A file copied by the FTP service into `/var/tmp` became visible at `/mnt/kenobi/tmp`.

This demonstrates how two otherwise separate services can be chained: FTP places a file; NFS provides access to the destination.

examples.title: Discover exports
examples.explanation: Request NFS-exported directories.

examples.title: Mount an export
examples.explanation: Attach remote /var to a local mount point.

pitfalls: NFS export visibility does not guarantee read or write permission for every file.

guides.title: SSH key-based authentication
guides.summary: A usable private key can authenticate a user when its matching public key is authorized.
takeaways: Knowing a key path is different from possessing the private key.
A private key must match an authorized public key; possession alone is not always sufficient.
guides.content:
## Kenobi example
`log.txt` revealed a path ending in `.ssh/id_rsa`. The private key itself was later obtained through the ProFTPD/NFS chain. The user successfully logged in as `kenobi` using `ssh -i`.

Keeping the private key's local file permissions restrictive (for example `chmod 600`) matters because OpenSSH may refuse insecurely accessible key files.

examples.title: Use a retrieved lab key
examples.explanation: Restrict access and identify which private key SSH should use.

pitfalls: Never commit private keys into a public repository or report.

guides.title: SUID menu analysis and PATH hijacking
guides.summary: A SUID program that resolves external command names through PATH can select an unintended executable.
takeaways: `strings` is a clue-finding tool, not source-code reconstruction.
`system()` invokes commands through a shell and can create command-resolution risk.
`export PATH=/home/kenobi/tools/:$PATH` adds a new first directory and preserves old ones.
guides.content:
## Discovery
Kenobi's custom `/usr/bin/menu` was SUID. `strings` exposed `setuid`, `system`, `curl -I localhost`, `uname -r`, and `ifconfig`. This suggested the program might launch shell commands by names rather than fixed paths.

## PATH lookup
The shell searches directories listed in `PATH` **left to right**. Adding a writable directory at the front can change which same-named executable is found. The effect on privileges depends on how the parent program launches the command and whether elevated identity is preserved.

**Current status:** learned with guidance; the learner explicitly wants more independent command-building practice. The submitted transcript does not include the final root-shell identity for this lab.

examples.title: Inspect command resolution
examples.explanation: Check search order and current executable location.

pitfalls: A matching string does not establish a vulnerable call path.
A PATH hijack only escalates privileges when the privileged execution conditions are present.

guides.title: Shell building blocks practiced
guides.summary: Basic Linux shell syntax needed to construct commands without relying on copy-paste.
takeaways: Prefer understanding each argument and operator instead of memorizing attack payloads.
guides.content:
## Building blocks
- `export VAR=value` makes a variable available to child processes.
- `$VAR` expands to the variable's existing value.
- `:` separates directories in `PATH`.
- `>` redirects standard output to a file; `2>&1` redirects standard error to the same output destination.
- `chmod +x` makes a script executable; `chmod 600` restricts a private key to its owner.
- `find / -perm -u=s -type f 2>/dev/null` searches for SUID files while suppressing errors.
- A here-document (`<<'EOF'`) is one way to write multi-line text into a script or service file.

The learner can explain `export PATH=/home/kenobi/tools/:$PATH` and wants more practice constructing scripts independently.

pitfalls: Changing PATH affects the current shell and exported child process environment, not other existing sessions.
